newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN PUBLIC SECTOR NEEDS PRIVATE HELP.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN PUBLIC SECTOR NEEDS PRIVATE HELP.

text.p: Public sector inefficiencies and funding constraints mean that the private sector should be welcomed into large infrastructural projects in the South African economy, a parliamentary finance comittee heard on Wednesday.

The committee was hearing from finance department officials and consultants who said they were advantages in so-called public-private sector partnerships (PPPs) despite the misgivings of some in government to private sector involvement.

"This is an extremely important area for government, particularly if government wants to deliver basic services in the next few years," chairman of the inter-governmental forum on PPPs Ismael Momoniat said.
He said it has been estimated that government would need at least 170 billion rand for infrastructure over the next five to 10 years, which government would be hard put to finance.
"That is probably the least important reason why we are going for private-public partnerships (PPPs)," he said.
"We must differentiate between the infrastructure that we are talking about and some of the big public enterprises like Eskom and Telkom," he said.
PPPs did not fall under the national framework agreement, through which unions have to be involved in the restructuring of state enterprises, because much of the infrastructure was new.
"I think that you would really be shocked to see how inefficient much of the public sector is in the delivery of services," Momoniat said.

For example, he said, he had visited an 80 million rand water and sewerage plant in Sebokeng. It was run by an electrician with no management skills. He did not know how much it cost to run the plant, half of which was not being used.
"It was a mess," he said, adding that it cried out for skilled private sector management.
Other infrastructural problems were equally plagued by inefficiences, wastages, excess capacity and the lack of maintenance.
The advantages of PPPs was that they could bring in new technology, create jobs through sub-contracting and improve efficiencies.

PPPs could take the form of management contracts, leasing agreements, concessioning and privatisation. But he and other speakers stressed that local communities would have to be involved and the projects closely monitored to ensure they met local need.
This would ensure that communities paid for the services provided.
